traditions/reformed/summary: The tradition originating with Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich (from 1519) and consolidated by John Calvin in Geneva, Heinrich Bullinger and others, expressed in confessions such as the Heidelberg Catechism (1563), the Belgic Confession and the Canons of Dort (1619). It stresses the sovereignty of God, the authority of Scripture and the reform of worship and church order according to the Word. Reformed churches spread across Switzerland, France (Huguenots), the Netherlands, Scotland, Hungary and, through migration and mission, to every continent.
traditions/reformed/distinctives/0: Sovereignty of God and the glory of God as the end of all things
traditions/reformed/distinctives/2: Worship regulated by Scripture, with emphasis on preaching
traditions/reformed/distinctives/3: Spiritual presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper
traditions/reformed/distinctives/4: Church discipline and ordered offices of pastor, elder and deacon
traditions/reformed/profile/authority: Scripture alone as the supreme rule of faith and life, illuminated by the Spirit, with subordinate confessional standards.
traditions/reformed/profile/salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's eternal election; the elect persevere.
traditions/reformed/profile/sacraments: Baptism (including infants of believers, as a sign of the covenant) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit.
traditions/reformed/profile/eschatology: Christ's return, resurrection and judgment; amillennial and postmillennial views historically predominant.
traditions/reformed/profile/governance: Presbyterian-synodal (rule by elders in consistories, classes and synods); some congregational variants.
traditions/reformed/profile/worship: Simple, Word-centred worship with psalm singing, preaching and prayer; historically without images.
traditions/reformed/profile/canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha excluded from Scripture.
traditions/reformed/status: Active; c. 100 million in WCRC member churches (2020), with additional conservative Reformed bodies.
traditions/presbyterian/summary: The English-speaking branch of the Reformed tradition, rooted in John Knox's Scottish Reformation (1560) and the Westminster Assembly (1643–1653), which produced the Westminster Confession and Catechisms. Named for government by presbyters (elders), Presbyterianism shaped Scotland, Ulster and colonial America, and through mission became strong in South Korea, Ghana, Malawi, Kenya, Brazil and north-east India. American Presbyterianism has repeatedly divided over revivalism, slavery, modernism and sexuality.
traditions/presbyterian/distinctives/0: Government by elders in sessions, presbyteries and general assemblies
traditions/presbyterian/distinctives/3: Strong emphasis on education and an educated ministry
traditions/presbyterian/distinctives/4: Major growth in Korea (e.g. Pyongyang revival, 1907)
traditions/presbyterian/profile/authorit: Scripture as the only infallible rule, with the Westminster Confession or other Reformed standards as subordinate standards.
traditions/presbyterian/profile/salvatio: Grace alone through faith alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and Christ's work; effectual calling, justification, adoption, sanctification.
traditions/presbyterian/profile/sacramen: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper as signs and seals of the covenant of grace.
traditions/presbyterian/profile/eschatol: Return of Christ, resurrection and last judgment; postmillennial hope was influential in the nineteenth century.
traditions/presbyterian/profile/governan: Presbyterian polity: teaching and ruling elders in graded courts.
traditions/presbyterian/profile/worship: Reformed worship ordered by the 'regulative principle' in conservative bodies; more varied in mainline churches.
traditions/presbyterian/status: Active; several tens of millions worldwide, with large churches in Korea, Africa and Brazil.
traditions/congregationalist/summary: A Reformed tradition holding that each gathered congregation of believers is a complete church under Christ, governing itself without bishops or presbyteries. It arose among English Separatists such as Robert Browne (1582) and the Pilgrims, and was established in Puritan New England, where it nurtured Harvard, Yale and the First Great Awakening (Jonathan Edwards). The Savoy Declaration (1658) adapted Westminster for Congregational polity. Many Congregationalist churches later merged into the United Church of Christ (US, 1957) and the United Reformed Church (UK, 1972).
traditions/congregationalist/distinctive: Autonomy of the local covenanted congregation
London Missionary Society (1795) and global missions
Influential role in American education and reform movements
traditions/congregationalist/profile/aut: Scripture, with historic Reformed confessions (e.g. the Savoy Declaration) held as testimonies rather than tests in many churches.
traditions/congregationalist/profile/sal: Historically Reformed teaching on grace and election; later wide theological diversity, including liberal Protestantism.
traditions/congregationalist/profile/sac: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper.
traditions/congregationalist/profile/esc: Historic Reformed hope; American Puritans often held a strong millennial expectation.
traditions/congregationalist/profile/gov: Congregational: each local church self-governing, linked in voluntary associations and councils.
traditions/congregationalist/profile/wor: Simple Reformed worship centred on preaching, in meeting houses.
traditions/congregationalist/status: Active, chiefly within united churches; independent Congregational bodies remain small.
traditions/anglican/summary: The churches descended from the Church of England, which broke with Rome when Henry VIII was declared Supreme Head (1534) and was reformed under Edward VI and Elizabeth I through Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer and the Thirty-nine Articles. Anglicans see themselves as both catholic and reformed, keeping the historic episcopate. Through colonial expansion and mission, Anglicanism became a worldwide communion of some 42 provinces, now with its largest membership in Nigeria, Uganda and Kenya. Debates over women's ordination and sexuality have produced realignments such as GAFCON (2008).
traditions/anglican/distinctives/0: Book of Common Prayer as a bond of unity
traditions/anglican/distinctives/1: Historic episcopate with Protestant doctrine (Thirty-nine Articles)
traditions/anglican/distinctives/2: Scripture, tradition and reason as sources of authority
traditions/anglican/distinctives/3: Breadth: Anglo-Catholic, evangelical and liberal wings
traditions/anglican/distinctives/4: Lambeth Conferences and the Archbishop of Canterbury as focus of unity
traditions/anglican/profile/authority: Scripture 'containeth all things necessary to salvation', read with the creeds, the early Fathers and reason; the Lambeth Quadrilateral (1888) summarises essentials.
traditions/anglican/profile/salvation: Justification by faith in Christ (Article XI), understood in a range from Reformed to catholic emphases.
traditions/anglican/profile/sacraments: Two dominical sacraments (baptism and Eucharist), with five other 'commonly called sacraments'; views of the Eucharist range widely.
traditions/anglican/profile/eschatology: The creeds' hope of Christ's return, resurrection and life everlasting; prayers for the dead in Anglo-Catholic use.
traditions/anglican/profile/governance: Episcopal and synodical; national provinces are autonomous, bound by 'bonds of affection' rather than central authority.
traditions/anglican/profile/worship: Common prayer: Morning and Evening Prayer and Holy Communion, with choral tradition and diverse modern rites.
traditions/anglican/profile/canon: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).
traditions/anglican/status: Active; c. 85 million members across about 42 provinces (2020).
traditions/anabaptist/summary: The 'radical' reformation that began when Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz and others in Zurich baptised one another as confessing believers in January 1525, breaking with Zwingli. Anabaptists ('rebaptisers', a name given by opponents) insisted on a voluntary church of committed disciples separate from the state. The Schleitheim Confession (1527) articulated nonresistance and refusal of oaths. Severely persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike, and discredited by the Münster episode (1534–1535), the movement survived as Mennonites, Hutterites and later Amish and Brethren.
traditions/anabaptist/distinctives/0: Believer's baptism on confession of faith
traditions/anabaptist/distinctives/1: The church as a voluntary, disciplined community of disciples
traditions/anabaptist/distinctives/2: Nonresistance and refusal of the sword
traditions/anabaptist/distinctives/3: Separation of church and state; refusal of oaths
traditions/anabaptist/profile/authority: Scripture, especially the New Testament and the Sermon on the Mount, interpreted in the gathered community under the Spirit.
traditions/anabaptist/profile/salvation: Grace received in faith that issues in a transformed life of obedient discipleship; salvation is not separable from following Christ.
traditions/anabaptist/profile/sacraments: Usually called ordinances: believer's baptism and the Lord's Supper as a memorial and community covenant meal; footwashing in some groups.
traditions/anabaptist/profile/eschatolog: Varied: some early leaders expected an imminent end; most later Anabaptists held a sober hope of Christ's return.
traditions/anabaptist/profile/governance: Congregational, with elected bishops/elders, ministers and deacons and mutual discipline (the 'ban').
traditions/anabaptist/profile/worship: Simple gatherings for Scripture, preaching, prayer and hymn singing (e.g. the Ausbund, from 1564).
traditions/anabaptist/profile/canon: The Protestant canon, with the Apocrypha valued by early Anabaptists.
traditions/anabaptist/status: Active as Mennonite, Amish, Hutterite and Brethren churches; c. 2.1 million baptised members in MWC-related churches (2022).
traditions/mennonite/summary: Anabaptist churches named after Menno Simons, a former Dutch Catholic priest who joined the movement in 1536 and gathered scattered communities in the Netherlands and northern Germany. The Dordrecht Confession (1632) became a standard. Mennonites migrated widely—to Prussia, Russia, North America and Paraguay—seeking religious freedom and exemption from military service. Today most Mennonites live in Africa, Asia and Latin America, with the largest national churches in Ethiopia (Meserete Kristos) and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
traditions/mennonite/distinctives/2: Service and relief work (Mennonite Central Committee, 1920)
traditions/mennonite/profile/authority: Scripture interpreted Christocentrically in community; confessions such as Dordrecht (1632) and the Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995).
traditions/mennonite/profile/salvation: Salvation by grace through faith expressed in discipleship, peacemaking and new life in Christ.
traditions/mennonite/profile/sacraments: Ordinances of believer's baptism, the Lord's Supper and, in many congregations, footwashing.
traditions/mennonite/profile/eschatology: Hope in Christ's return and the fulfilment of God's kingdom of peace.
traditions/mennonite/profile/governance: Congregational with regional conferences; pastors and elders chosen by congregations.
traditions/mennonite/profile/worship: Simple services with preaching and often unaccompanied four-part singing.
traditions/mennonite/status: Active; the majority of the c. 2.1 million Anabaptist-related believers worldwide.
traditions/amish/summary: A conservative Anabaptist fellowship that separated from Swiss and Alsatian Mennonites in 1693 under Jakob Ammann, who called for stricter shunning (Meidung) of excommunicated members and more frequent communion. Amish migrated to Pennsylvania from the 1730s and now live almost entirely in the United States and Canada. Known for plain dress, horse-and-buggy transport and selective use of technology, they have one of the fastest population growth rates of any religious group, doubling roughly every twenty years.
traditions/amish/distinctives/0: Ordnung: unwritten community rules governing dress and technology
traditions/amish/distinctives/2: Gelassenheit: yieldedness to God and community
traditions/amish/distinctives/3: Pennsylvania German language and home-based worship
traditions/amish/distinctives/4: Education through eighth grade in community schools
traditions/amish/profile/authority: Scripture, the Dordrecht Confession (1632) and the church district's Ordnung.
traditions/amish/profile/salvation: Grace received in humble faith and obedience; Amish typically speak of a 'living hope' of salvation rather than assurance.
traditions/amish/profile/sacraments: Adult baptism on joining the church (usually aged 16–25), twice-yearly communion with footwashing.
traditions/amish/profile/eschatology: Hope of eternal life and Christ's return, with little speculative interest.
traditions/amish/profile/governance: Autonomous church districts led by a bishop, ministers and a deacon chosen by lot.
traditions/amish/profile/worship: Three-hour services every other Sunday in members' homes, with slow unison hymns from the Ausbund.
traditions/amish/profile/canon: The Luther Bible (High German) and the Protestant canon.
traditions/amish/status: Active; c. 400,000 people including children (2024), in over 600 settlements.
